what_it_does: Vision Transformers — a type of AI model that processes images by splitting them into patches and letting every patch attend to every other patch — have a costly "attention" step whose work grows as the square of the number of patches, making them far too slow for dense image-understanding tasks (like segmenting every pixel) on small, low-power edge devices. This paper proposes a new attention design called Decoupled Chunk Attention, which breaks the image into manageable chunks and processes them in a pipeline so that far less data needs to travel to the slow off-chip memory. The hardware pairs two kinds of on-chip memory: fast, volatile storage (SRAM — think of it as a small, quick scratch-pad) and slower but persistent, non-volatile storage (RRAM — a type of memory that keeps its contents without power). Reconfigurable compute units inside those memory chips can be switched between different operating modes to handle the varying work sizes that arise when a Transformer is built in a pyramid shape (processing images at multiple resolutions). The result is a chip design claimed to reduce off-chip memory traffic and energy while keeping the accuracy needed for edge vision tasks.
